questions.stem: On the continuum of arousal, which state lies at the opposite end from deep sleep?
options: relaxed wakefulness
drowsiness
light sleep
hyperarousal
questions.explanation: The continuum of arousal runs from deep sleep, through light sleep, drowsiness and relaxed and alert wakefulness, to hyperarousal, an extremely heightened state such as panic. Drowsiness and light sleep sit close to the low-arousal end.

questions.stem: Jun is sitting a difficult exam. He feels alert and focused, but not panicked. Where is he on the continuum of arousal?
options: in drowsiness, just between light sleep and relaxed wakefulness
in alert wakefulness, between relaxed wakefulness and hyperarousal
in hyperarousal, at the highest end of the continuum of arousal
in relaxed wakefulness, close to drowsiness and light sleep
questions.explanation: Focused alertness without panic is a moderately high level of arousal, above relaxed wakefulness but short of hyperarousal. Hyperarousal involves an extreme level of arousal, such as panic, that usually impairs performance.

questions.stem: In psychology, selective attention refers to the ability to:
options: attend to two or more tasks at the same time
stay awake and alert for long periods
switch rapidly between sleep and waking
focus on one stimulus while ignoring others
questions.explanation: Selective attention means concentrating on one source of information, such as a friend's voice at a noisy party, while filtering out the rest. Attending to two or more tasks at once is divided attention.

questions.stem: Mia can easily walk and chat to a friend at the same time, but she struggles to write an essay while listening to a podcast. What best explains the difference?
options: Selective attention fails her whenever she tries to listen to any spoken words
Divided attention is easier when one task is automatic and the tasks are dissimilar
Divided attention is easier when both of the tasks are new and need careful thought
Selective attention allows her to do any two tasks at once with practice
questions.explanation: Walking is a well-practised, automatic task, so it takes little attention, leaving capacity for conversation. Writing and listening to speech both demand controlled processing of language, so they compete for the same limited capacity.

questions.stem: Craik and colleagues (1996) had participants learn word lists while sometimes also doing a second task. Which finding did they report?
options: Dividing attention had no effect on memory whether it occurred at learning or at recall
Dividing attention improved memory by keeping participants more alert during the task
Dividing attention while learning reduced later recall far more than dividing it at recall
Dividing attention at recall reduced memory far more than dividing it while learning
questions.explanation: Craik and colleagues found that a secondary task during encoding greatly reduced later memory, while a secondary task during retrieval had a much smaller effect on accuracy, although it slowed performance on the secondary task. Attention is therefore especially important when information is first learnt.

questions.stem: In the Stroop task (Stroop 1935), participants name the ink colour of colour words. Why does naming the ink colour of 'RED' printed in green ink take longer than naming a green patch?
options: Colour words are processed by the brain only after the ink colour is named
Automatic reading of the word interferes with naming the ink colour
The green ink is harder to see when it is printed as a word
Participants must divide attention between three tasks at once
questions.explanation: Reading is so practised that it happens automatically, and the word 'red' competes with the response 'green', slowing it down. This interference from incongruent information is the Stroop effect.

questions.stem: A student replicates the Stroop effect. Her independent variable is whether colour words are printed in matching or mismatching ink. Which is the most suitable dependent variable?
options: The number of colour words included in each of the lists
The age and gender of each participant in the investigation
The time taken to name the ink colours in each list
Whether the words are printed in matching or mismatching ink
questions.explanation: The dependent variable is what is measured, here the processing time for naming ink colours, which should be longer for mismatching (incongruent) words. Whether the ink matches is the independent variable, and the number of words should be controlled.

questions.stem: How do the hypothalamus and the pineal gland interact to regulate sleep?
options: The hypothalamus detects darkness and signals the pineal gland to release melatonin
The pineal gland detects light and signals the hypothalamus to release adrenaline
The hypothalamus releases melatonin, which signals the pineal gland to wake the body
The pineal gland detects darkness and signals the hypothalamus to release cortisol
questions.explanation: The suprachiasmatic nucleus in the hypothalamus receives information about light from the eyes. As light fades it signals the pineal gland to secrete melatonin, which promotes sleepiness. The pineal gland, not the hypothalamus, releases melatonin.

questions.stem: Melatonin levels in the blood are normally highest:
options: in the early afternoon
just after waking in the morning
during bright midday sunlight
during the night, in darkness
questions.explanation: Melatonin is secreted as light fades and stays high through the night, helping maintain sleep; bright light suppresses it. Levels fall towards morning, which helps us wake.

questions.stem: While reading in a busy library, Tara suddenly hears her own name across the room and turns towards it. Which interaction best explains how her attention shifted?
options: The reticular formation raised arousal, the thalamus relayed the sound, and the cortex focused on it
The pineal gland raised arousal, the hypothalamus relayed the sound, and the cortex focused on it
The cortex relayed the sound, the thalamus raised arousal, and the reticular formation focused on it
The cerebellum raised arousal, the medulla relayed the sound, and the thalamus focused on it
questions.explanation: The reticular formation regulates arousal and alertness, the thalamus relays sensory information to the cortex and helps filter it, and the cortex directs conscious attention to the important stimulus. The pineal gland and hypothalamus regulate the sleep-wake cycle, not the moment-to-moment focus of attention.

questions.stem: Damage to the reticular formation is most likely to cause:
options: a loss of the ability to produce fluent speech
an inability to recognise familiar faces at all
a loss of fine control of the hand movements
a severe reduction in arousal, possibly a coma
questions.explanation: The reticular formation, running through the brainstem, maintains arousal and wakefulness, so serious damage can leave a person unable to be roused. Speech production and face recognition depend on cortical areas.

questions.stem: Which device records the electrical activity of the muscles, such as muscle tone in the chin during sleep?
options: electrooculograph (EOG)
positron emission tomography (PET)
electromyograph (EMG)
electroencephalograph (EEG)
questions.explanation: An EMG detects the electrical activity of muscles. An EEG records brain waves and an EOG records eye movements.

questions.stem: What does an electrooculograph (EOG) measure?
options: the electrical activity of neurons in the visual cortex
the amount of light that enters through the pupil of the eye
the blood flow to brain areas that process vision
the electrical activity of the muscles that move the eyes
questions.explanation: The EOG uses electrodes near the eyes to record eye movements, which are rapid in REM sleep and slow and rolling at sleep onset. Activity in the visual cortex would be part of an EEG recording.

questions.stem: A participant's recordings show fast, low-amplitude brain waves, almost no muscle tone in the chin and bursts of rapid eye movement. What state is the participant most likely in?
options: REM sleep
deep NREM sleep
alert wakefulness
drowsy relaxation
questions.explanation: In REM sleep the EEG looks similar to wakefulness, but the EMG shows near loss of muscle tone and the EOG shows rapid eye movements. Awake people have normal muscle tone, and deep NREM sleep has slow, high-amplitude waves.

questions.stem: In deep NREM sleep, the EEG mainly shows:
options: alpha waves mixed with rapid eye movements
irregular waves with frequent eye movements
slow, high-amplitude delta waves
fast, low-amplitude beta waves
questions.explanation: The deepest stage of NREM sleep, also called slow-wave sleep, is dominated by delta waves of high amplitude and low frequency. Fast, low-amplitude waves occur in alert wakefulness and REM sleep.

questions.stem: In a healthy adult, how does a night's sleep usually change from early to late in the night?
options: Each cycle contains roughly equal amounts of deep NREM and REM sleep
Deep NREM and REM sleep both disappear after the first two cycles
Deep NREM sleep dominates early cycles; REM periods get longer later
REM sleep dominates early cycles; deep NREM sleep gets longer later
questions.explanation: Sleep cycles last about 90 minutes. Early cycles contain most of the night's deep NREM sleep, while REM periods lengthen in later cycles, so most REM sleep occurs towards morning.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts REM and NREM sleep?
options: REM shows slow delta waves; NREM shows fast waves like those of wakefulness
REM involves vivid dreams and muscle paralysis; NREM includes the deepest sleep
NREM involves vivid dreams and muscle paralysis; REM includes the deepest sleep
REM occurs only at the start of the night; NREM occurs only towards morning
questions.explanation: REM sleep is linked to vivid dreaming, with the body's skeletal muscles largely paralysed, while NREM sleep moves from light stages into deep slow-wave sleep. Delta waves belong to deep NREM sleep, not REM.

questions.stem: According to the restoration theory, we sleep in order to:
options: stay safe from predators during the dark hours of the night
save energy when food is scarce and hunting is difficult
process the emotions experienced during the previous day
recover and repair the body and brain after daily activity
questions.explanation: Restoration theory proposes that sleep lets the body and brain recover, for example by repairing tissue and replenishing resources used while awake. Staying safe and saving energy are explanations from evolutionary theory.

questions.stem: Large grazing animals such as horses sleep only a few hours a day, while lions sleep for many hours. Which theory of sleep explains this difference best?
options: Restoration theory, because grazing animals do less physical work than lions
Restoration theory, because lions need more time to replace their muscle tissue
Evolutionary theory, because all animals sleep the same amount when they are safe
Evolutionary theory, because sleep patterns suit each species' survival needs
questions.explanation: Evolutionary theory proposes that sleep patterns evolved to aid survival. Grazing prey animals need long periods awake to eat and watch for predators, whereas lions can eat quickly and have few predators, so long sleep carries little risk.

questions.stem: Which observation is better explained by restoration theory than by evolutionary theory?
options: Humans sleep at night, when moving around in the dark would be most risky
People tend to sleep longer and more deeply after a day of heavy physical exertion
Most animals sleep at times when they would be most at risk of attack
Prey animals tend to sleep for shorter periods than predators do
questions.explanation: If sleep exists to restore the body, more exertion should create more need for sleep, which fits sleeping longer after heavy activity. Sleeping when at most risk, and prey sleeping less than predators, are explained by evolutionary theory.

questions.stem: Compared with adults, newborn babies:
options: sleep for more hours and spend a higher proportion of sleep in REM
sleep for fewer hours and spend a lower proportion of sleep in REM
sleep for more hours but spend almost no time in REM sleep
sleep for fewer hours but spend most of that sleep in deep NREM
questions.explanation: Newborns sleep around 16 hours a day, and about half of it is REM sleep, compared with roughly a fifth to a quarter in adults. Total sleep time and the proportion of REM both decrease through childhood.

questions.stem: What is the sleep-wake shift in adolescence?
options: A large drop in the total amount of sleep adolescents need each night
A change from mostly REM sleep to mostly NREM sleep each night
A delay in the timing of melatonin release, so adolescents feel sleepy later at night
An advance in the timing of melatonin release, so adolescents feel sleepy earlier at night
questions.explanation: During adolescence melatonin is released later in the evening than in childhood, so teenagers do not feel sleepy until later but still need around 8 to 10 hours of sleep. Early school starts can therefore cause partial sleep deprivation.

questions.stem: A high school is deciding whether to start classes at 9:30 am rather than 8:30 am. Which argument is best supported by sleep research?
options: A later start is unhelpful because adolescents need less sleep than adults
An earlier start helps because adolescents' melatonin is released earlier at night
Start times make no difference because sleep timing is set by willpower alone
A later start fits adolescents' delayed sleep timing, so they may get more sleep
questions.explanation: Because adolescents' melatonin release is delayed, they tend to fall asleep late; a later start lets them sleep longer before school. This is an example of sleep research informing policy. Adolescents need more sleep than adults, not less, and their melatonin is released later, not earlier.

questions.stem: Which change in sleep is typical of older adults compared with young adults?
options: more deep NREM sleep and fewer awakenings during the night
a much higher proportion of REM sleep than in childhood
a delay in sleep timing, so that they tend to go to bed much later
less deep NREM sleep and more frequent waking during the night
questions.explanation: With age, the amount of deep slow-wave sleep falls and sleep becomes more broken, with more awakenings. Older adults also tend to feel sleepy earlier in the evening, the opposite of the adolescent delay.

questions.stem: What is the difference between total and partial sleep deprivation?
options: Total is less sleep than needed; partial is no sleep at all for a period
Total is missing REM sleep only; partial is missing NREM sleep only
Total lasts for one night only; partial lasts for more than one week
Total is no sleep at all for a period; partial is less sleep than needed
questions.explanation: Total sleep deprivation means going without any sleep, for example staying awake all night. Partial sleep deprivation means getting less sleep than needed, in quantity or quality, which is common among adolescents.

questions.stem: After several nights of only five hours' sleep, Kai has trouble concentrating in class and feels irritable and low. These effects are best described as:
options: physical consequences of total sleep deprivation
symptoms of narcolepsy caused by too much REM sleep
symptoms of sleep apnoea caused by a blocked airway
psychological consequences of partial sleep deprivation
questions.explanation: Poor concentration and low, irritable mood are psychological effects, and repeatedly sleeping less than needed is partial sleep deprivation. Total deprivation means no sleep at all. Physical effects would include fatigue, headaches or reduced immunity.

questions.stem: Which is a physical, rather than psychological, consequence of sleep deprivation?
options: reduced immune function
lowered, irritable mood
poorer concentration
slower decision-making
questions.explanation: Weakened immunity is a physical effect on the body. Mood, concentration and decision-making are psychological effects on emotion and thinking.

questions.stem: Workplaces such as hospitals and transport companies limit shift lengths and require rest breaks. What understanding of sleep is this policy based on?
options: Sleep deprivation improves alertness over time as workers adapt to long shifts
Sleep deprivation affects mood only, so its main risk is conflict between colleagues at work
Sleep deprivation only matters if a worker misses more than one night's sleep
Sleep deprivation impairs concentration and judgement, which raises the risk of accidents
questions.explanation: Lack of sleep reduces concentration, slows reactions and impairs judgement, so fatigue is managed as a workplace risk. Even one night of lost sleep or ongoing partial loss can impair performance, and people do not adapt fully to deprivation.

questions.stem: Sleep-onset insomnia is a sleep disorder in which a person:
options: stops breathing repeatedly during sleep
falls asleep suddenly during the daytime
walks around while in deep sleep
has persistent difficulty falling asleep
questions.explanation: Sleep-onset insomnia is ongoing difficulty getting to sleep, despite the opportunity to sleep. Repeated pauses in breathing describe sleep apnoea, and sudden daytime sleep attacks are typical of narcolepsy.

questions.stem: Dan snores loudly, his partner notices he stops breathing many times each night, and he is very sleepy during the day. Which sleep disorder is most likely?
options: sleepwalking
sleep apnoea
narcolepsy
sleep-onset insomnia
questions.explanation: In obstructive sleep apnoea the airway repeatedly closes during sleep, breathing stops, and the person briefly wakes to breathe again, often with loud snoring. The broken sleep causes daytime sleepiness, even though the person may not remember waking.

questions.stem: Lucy has sudden attacks of sleep during the day, and when she laughs her muscles suddenly go weak. Which disorder do these symptoms suggest?
options: sleep apnoea
sleep-onset insomnia
sleepwalking
narcolepsy
questions.explanation: Narcolepsy involves excessive daytime sleepiness and sudden sleep attacks, and often cataplexy, a sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotions such as laughter. People with narcolepsy can enter REM sleep unusually quickly.

questions.stem: Sleepwalking usually occurs in the first part of the night. Which explanation is consistent with sleep stage research?
options: It occurs during REM sleep, which is concentrated early in the night
It occurs during deep NREM sleep, which is concentrated late in the night
It occurs during REM sleep, when the muscles are most active
It occurs during deep NREM sleep, which is concentrated early in the night
questions.explanation: Sleepwalking arises from deep NREM sleep, which dominates the first sleep cycles. During REM sleep the skeletal muscles are largely paralysed, which normally prevents acting out movements.

questions.stem: Which is a behavioural part of cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I)?
options: Exposure to bright light in the early morning on waking
Getting out of bed if not asleep within about 20 minutes
Replacing the thought 'I'll fail tomorrow if I don't sleep'
Taking sleeping tablets nightly before going to bed
questions.explanation: CBT-I includes stimulus control, such as leaving the bed when unable to sleep so the bed becomes linked with sleep rather than wakefulness. Challenging unhelpful thoughts about sleep is the cognitive part, and bright light therapy is a separate treatment.

questions.stem: In CBT-I, a therapist helps Sara challenge her belief that one bad night will ruin her whole week. This targets:
options: the timing of her melatonin release through light
her muscle tone during REM sleep each night
the breathing problems that wake her during sleep
unhelpful thoughts that increase anxiety about sleep
questions.explanation: The cognitive part of CBT-I identifies and changes unhelpful, anxious beliefs about sleep that keep a person aroused at bedtime. Shifting melatonin timing is the aim of bright light therapy.

questions.stem: Ollie has a delayed sleep phase: he cannot fall asleep until 2 am and struggles to wake for school. Which bright light therapy plan is most appropriate?
options: Bright light late in the evening, and dark sunglasses in the morning
Bright light at midnight, then complete darkness until midday
Dim light all day, then bright light just before going to bed
Bright light soon after waking in the morning, and dim light in the evening
questions.explanation: Morning bright light shifts the body clock earlier, so melatonin is released earlier in the evening, and avoiding bright evening light stops it being delayed further. Evening bright light would delay his sleep even more; that approach suits an advanced sleep phase.

questions.stem: A survey of 120 students finds a correlation of r = -0.62 between minutes spent reading on electronic devices in bed and hours of sleep. What does this show?
options: More device reading is associated with more hours of sleep
Device reading and sleep hours show no relationship at all
More device reading is associated with fewer hours of sleep
More device reading causes students to sleep for fewer hours
questions.explanation: A negative r means that as one variable increases the other tends to decrease, and -0.62 is a moderate to strong relationship. Correlational research cannot show cause, because a third variable such as stress could affect both.

questions.stem: A study finds that students who exercise more during the day sleep longer at night (r = +0.45). Which conclusion is valid?
options: Exercise and sleep are strongly related, because any r above zero is strong
Longer sleep causes students to exercise more on the following day, as r is positive
Exercise and sleep duration are moderately positively related, but cause cannot be inferred
Exercise causes longer sleep, because the correlation is positive and moderate
questions.explanation: An r of +0.45 is a moderate positive relationship: more exercise tends to go with more sleep. Because the variables were measured, not manipulated, the study cannot show that either one causes the other.
